video_title: Why Only Issuers Should Be Able to Tokenize Stock, Says Carlos Domingo
gist: Securitize CEO Carlos Domingo explains why the company both listed on the NYSE and tokenized its own SECZ shares on Solana and Avalanche, and argues that only issuers (working through SEC-regulated transfer agents) should be able to tokenize stock — offshore 'tokenized equity' being debt derivatives that break corporate-action, insider-trading and OFAC guardrails. He also flags an underappreciated catalyst: the SEC's proposal to repeal Rule 611, which would free onchain equity venues from having to mirror the NBBO tape via an oracle.

themes.theme: Dual-track IPO: NYSE listing plus onchain shares

insights.claim: Securitize deliberately did both a traditional NYSE listing and an onchain tokenization of more than $265 million of its own stock because the tokenized equity market does not yet have enough liquidity to support an IPO or listing on its own.
insights.speaker: Carlos Domingo
insights.so_what: Tokenized equity is an additive distribution channel, not a near-term replacement for exchange listings — model it as incremental venue optionality rather than a threat to NYSE/Nasdaq volumes.
insights.quote: I don't think that today the the tokenized equity market is ready for just only be traded on chain. I don't think there is enough liquidity.

insights.claim: The genuine equity-tokenization market where the token actually represents equity — Securitize, Figure and Superstate — is only around $600 million, while offshore derivative 'tokenized stock' is roughly double that size.
insights.speaker: Carlos Domingo
insights.so_what: Sizes the entire real tokenized-equity TAM at under $1B today, so headline 'tokenized stock' volumes are mostly synthetic exposure, not issuer-sanctioned equity.
insights.quote: us and figure and superstate which are the only ones that doing like real tokenization where the token does represent equity is is around I don't know $600 million or something like that

insights.claim: Securitize started its go-public process only after seeing the crypto IPO window reopen post-Circle, with Gemini, eToro and BitGo also planning listings, and bankers confirming the market was open.
insights.speaker: Carlos Domingo
insights.so_what: Confirms a live crypto IPO cohort forming behind Circle — watch for a supply wave of listed crypto-infrastructure comps that will set valuation anchors for tokenization businesses.
insights.quote: the IPO market was open for crypto companies after many years as you know that you know since the Coinbase IPO I guess that there was no other uh you know crypto IPOs except for for miners

insights.claim: Domingo expects crypto M&A to accelerate specifically because more crypto companies are now publicly traded, since a market-set stock price and liquid currency make acquisitions far easier than swapping private shares.
insights.speaker: Carlos Domingo
insights.so_what: Newly listed crypto equities become acquisition currency — expect consolidation to concentrate in the listed cohort, making listed names the likely consolidators of private crypto assets.
insights.quote: when you're private, it's a lot more difficult to acquire another company. When you're public, the price of your company is is set by the market.

insights.claim: Having gone through the process, Domingo says the US IPO regulatory and disclosure burden was longer and more expensive than he expected and publicly backs SEC Chair Atkins' push to simplify disclosures to get companies public earlier.
insights.speaker: Carlos Domingo
insights.so_what: If disclosure simplification lands, the stay-private-longer regime could partially reverse — a structural positive for IPO-linked intermediaries and a negative for late-stage private markets.
insights.quote: I didn't expect that it was going to be such a long process and I know Chair Atkins is saying that we need to simplify disclosures and and and the IPO process to stimulate more companies going public

themes.theme: Native tokenization vs offshore equity derivatives

insights.claim: Most offshore 'tokenized stocks' are structured as debt instruments against an SPV or broker dealer holding the underlying shares, so holders are not on the cap table, carry counterparty risk, and may not receive dividends if they never did KYC.
insights.speaker: Carlos Domingo
insights.so_what: Investors buying offshore tokenized equities are underwriting an unrated credit exposure to an opaque issuer, not equity — a hidden risk if any of these venues fails.
insights.quote: They're misled because the they are showing this as tokenized equities, but it's not a tokenized equity. You're getting a debt instrument

insights.claim: Domingo cites a real failure where an offshore issuer's tokenized Netflix stock did not process the Netflix stock split, leaving the onchain version trading at a five-times different price from the real shares.
insights.speaker: Carlos Domingo
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence that corporate-action handling — not custody — is the breaking point for derivative tokenized equity; a checklist item for anyone diligencing these products.
insights.quote: they actually issued this tokenized uh equity for I I believe it was for Netflix and then Netflix did an split and then the the the onchain version did not do the split and they were trading at five times different price

insights.claim: Domingo rejects the claim that tokenized equity cannot legally be done in the US, saying Securitize proved native equity tokenization, US issuance and onchain trading are all doable under existing regulation and licenses.
insights.speaker: Carlos Domingo
insights.so_what: Removes the main public justification for offshore structures, raising the odds regulators eventually treat them as deliberate arbitrage rather than necessity.
insights.quote: These are people playing regulatory arbitrage that they just don't want to do it following the the existing regulations in in the US.

insights.claim: Domingo argues the offshore model is not driven by crypto's permissionless ethos at all, since the tokens are distributed through centralized offshore exchanges that even let Chinese users connect via VPNs to trade US stock derivatives.
insights.speaker: Carlos Domingo
insights.so_what: Reframes the decentralization defense as a business-model choice, which is how regulators are likely to view it — elevating enforcement risk for the venues involved.
insights.quote: this notion of permissionless and censorship resistant this these things are issued through centralized offshore exchanges there's nothing decentralized there

themes.theme: The issuer-authorization fight at the SEC

insights.claim: Securitize sits on the board of the Securities Transfer Association and backs its position to the SEC that tokenized securities should require authorization from the underlying issuer.
insights.speaker: Carlos Domingo
insights.so_what: If the SEC adopts issuer-authorization, transfer agents and issuer-sponsored platforms like Securitize become the mandatory chokepoint and offshore derivative issuers lose their product.
insights.quote: issuers need to be able to control what happens with their securities with their company name with their QIPS and they need to authorize what you do

insights.claim: Domingo relays Bullish CEO Tom Farley's point that permissionless offshore derivatives of a company's own equity let insiders such as a CFO trade anonymously the day before earnings, breaking insider-trading rules the issuer is responsible for.
insights.speaker: Carlos Domingo
insights.so_what: Gives issuers a compliance-driven reason to actively fight unauthorized tokenization, which is a stronger lobbying force than the crypto-native counterargument.
insights.quote: my CFO let's say can go there and buy or sell those those derivatives completely anonymously the day before the earning announcements

insights.claim: Domingo notes Coinbase and Robinhood have not tokenized their own equity, yet roughly five different unauthorized derivative versions of each already exist, issued without either company's permission and sometimes listing the real CUSIP.
insights.speaker: Carlos Domingo
insights.so_what: Quantifies the trademark and CUSIP-misuse exposure large issuers face, which is the wedge likely to bring listed crypto companies onto the pro-authorization side.
insights.quote: there is five different versions of derivatives of Robin Hood equity or or Coinbase equity that have been issued completely without Coinbase permission

themes.theme: Rule 611, the NBBO oracle, and onchain price formation

insights.claim: Because of the national best bid and offer rule, Securitize's onchain shares must trade at exactly the same price as on Robinhood during market hours, eliminating any onchain-versus-offchain price discount or premium.
insights.speaker: Carlos Domingo
insights.so_what: Kills the arbitrage trade many expect between tokenized and traditional shares during regular hours — the only real spread opportunity is outside market hours.
insights.quote: So whether you trade them on Robin Hood or you trade them on on our uh you know propm technology with Jam you're going to get the same price.

insights.claim: Securitize enforces NBBO compliance by injecting the real-time SIP tape price on chain as an oracle that the market maker reads, effectively making the onchain venue a price-taker from the national market system.
insights.speaker: Carlos Domingo
insights.so_what: Today's tokenized equity venues are technically dependent on TradFi price feeds — an architectural constraint that limits how 'crypto-native' these markets can be until Rule 611 changes.
insights.quote: what we do is we actually inject the the the the real-time pricing on chain for you know jump to be able to read it and offer you that

insights.claim: The SEC has published a document proposing to repeal Rule 611, the 2005 order protection rule, and Domingo says crypto markets have almost entirely missed how consequential this is for onchain equity trading.
insights.speaker: Carlos Domingo
insights.so_what: A repeal would let onchain equity venues form their own prices and let market makers arbitrage spreads for profit — the single biggest regulatory catalyst for tokenized equity liquidity.
insights.quote: it's actually pretty relevant for crypto because it means we'll be able to trade on chain at whatever price it trades on chain and not have to like do this convoluted process

insights.claim: Securitize's tokenized shares currently trade extended hours rather than 24/7, and outside market hours there is no price protection at all, so both onchain and offchain investors face thin liquidity and worse execution.
insights.speaker: Carlos Domingo
insights.so_what: Tempers the 24/7 tokenization pitch — the real constraint on continuous equity trading is liquidity, not technology, so early tokenized markets will have wide overnight spreads.
insights.quote: We actually trade extended hours, not 247 yet, but we're working on enablement that.

themes.theme: Three ownership models and the transfer agent chokepoint

insights.claim: There are three distinct tokenized-stock models: issuer-sponsored tokenization through a transfer agent whose ledger is a blockchain, DTCC-style tokenized entitlements, and offshore debt derivatives — and only the first puts the buyer on the actual cap table with full rights.
insights.speaker: Carlos Domingo
insights.so_what: The cleanest taxonomy for diligencing any 'tokenized stock' product — ask which of the three it is before assessing rights, custody and counterparty risk.
insights.quote: the transfer agent happens to use a blockchain as their underlying ledger and therefore you get a token as the entry on that ledger right which is what what a blockchain is

insights.claim: Investors buying stock on Robinhood receive only an entitlement to shares held at DTCC rather than the shares themselves, so the issuer literally does not know those holders exist and cannot conduct corporate actions with them directly.
insights.speaker: Carlos Domingo
insights.so_what: Explains the structural pitch for issuer-sponsored tokenization: direct cap-table visibility is a genuine product improvement issuers will pay for, not just a crypto talking point.
insights.quote: When somebody has shares on Robin Hood, we don't even know they exist because they're not on the on the cap table.

insights.claim: The SEC-regulated transfer agent is the mandatory gatekeeper for any issuer wanting to tokenize its stock, and Computershare, Equiniti and Continental control the large majority of US publicly traded equity — with Equiniti in the process of being acquired by Bullish.
insights.speaker: Carlos Domingo
insights.so_what: Transfer agents are the scarce bottleneck asset in equity tokenization — Bullish buying Equiniti signals crypto firms competing to own that layer rather than route around it.
insights.quote: the transfer agents are computer share. Um you know equinity computer has partnered with us. Equinity has is in the process of being acquired by bullies as you know. Continental is also partner with us

insights.claim: Securitize had to buy shares off the open market via a broker dealer and move them outside DTCC to put them on chain, at which point they escape traditional market structure and can be traded, settled instantly and later used as DeFi collateral.
insights.speaker: Carlos Domingo
insights.so_what: Moving shares out of DTCC is the technical unlock that separates real tokenization from wrapped entitlements — and it is what makes equities usable as DeFi collateral.
insights.quote: So everything that is on DTCC trades through the existing market structure right exchanges the broker dealers etc. So once you move them on chain they're kind of outside of that scope.

insights.claim: Because natively tokenized shares are permissioned securities with the holder on the cap table, Securitize can verify a holder who loses their wallet keys, burn the old shares and reissue new tokens — removing the irreversible-loss risk of bearer crypto assets.
insights.speaker: Carlos Domingo
insights.so_what: Undercuts the main custody objection to onchain securities for institutions and retail alike; permissioning is a feature for regulated assets, not a compromise.
insights.quote: if you you were to lose the keys of your wallet, we'll be able to verify that you were an investor and reissue burn the old shares and and reissue the the new tokenized shares

themes.theme: NYSE digital ATS versus the DTCC approach

insights.claim: The New York Stock Exchange is standing up a digital ATS to trade tokenized securities with Securitize as design partner, targeting a Q4 launch, with Securitize approved both as transfer agent to send tokenized equities and ETFs there and as the broker dealer through which retail must access it.
insights.speaker: Carlos Domingo
insights.so_what: A dated, named catalyst: a Q4 NYSE digital ATS launch would be the first large-scale regulated onchain equity venue and a step change in institutional tokenization adoption.
insights.quote: they've announced that they're launching in in in Q4. uh we're working towards that uh that deadline

insights.claim: Domingo treats the NYSE building an onchain venue as third-party validation that instant settlement and 24/7 trading have real value, since the world's largest exchange would not otherwise invest in it.
insights.speaker: Carlos Domingo
insights.so_what: Incumbent-exchange participation de-risks the tokenization thesis for allocators who were waiting for a credible non-crypto sponsor.
insights.quote: the fact that they actually do see a future of onchain trading where you have you know 247 where you have instant settlement etc. It's uh it's very interesting because it somehow validates the thesis that there is value there

insights.claim: DTCC's tokenized entitlements will only move between wallets of approved clearing participants and still clear T+1, so they deliver back-office efficiency for broker dealers rather than instant settlement or a new onchain ecosystem.
insights.speaker: Carlos Domingo
insights.so_what: DTCC's entry legitimizes the word tokenization but does not compete for the DeFi-collateral use case — the two models address different markets and both can win.
insights.quote: it's going to clear the plus one. So it's not going to do like uh instant clearing, instant settlement or or 247.

themes.theme: Institutional adoption blockers and Securitize's capital roadmap

insights.claim: Large asset managers exploring tokenization are gated by two concerns — regulatory exposure that could threaten their far larger core business, and reputational risk from assets trading in permissionless venues accessible to sanctioned actors.
insights.speaker: Carlos Domingo
insights.so_what: Compliance and brand risk, not technology, is the binding constraint on institutional RWA volumes — so regulated permissioned rails will capture institutional flow ahead of permissionless ones.
insights.quote: it's a combination of regulatory and um and and reputational uh in terms of getting into crypto

insights.claim: Domingo says a top-three US bank walked away from a signed tokenization project with Securitize in 2021 after the FTX, Celsius and BlockFi failures, purely to avoid being associated with the sector in press coverage.
insights.speaker: Carlos Domingo
insights.so_what: Concrete precedent that a single sector blowup can freeze institutional tokenization pipelines for years — the key downside scenario for RWA growth forecasts.
insights.quote: we don't want to be on a you know on the Wall Street Journal article saying oh we've tokenized this with securityize and you know this guy is going to jail and the other guy is going to jail

insights.claim: Domingo's biggest stated worry for tokenization is that one of the unregulated offshore products blows up, repeating the Celsius and BlockFi pattern and causing large institutions to pull back from the entire space.
insights.speaker: Carlos Domingo
insights.so_what: A specific contagion channel to monitor: an offshore tokenized-equity failure would be a sector-wide de-rating event for RWA infrastructure names, including Securitize itself.
insights.quote: one of the things worries me is that one of these things blows up, right? Because these things are completely unregulated. They're done offshore without any controls, distributed by people without licenses

insights.claim: Securitize chose Avalanche and Solana for its own stock partly because both offer deterministic settlement — which Domingo says L2s lack and which creates a real regulatory problem, since a trade that must be reported and then unwinds is a compliance failure.
insights.speaker: Carlos Domingo
insights.so_what: Deterministic finality becomes a hard selection criterion for regulated securities issuance, structurally disadvantaging optimistic-rollup L2s for tokenized equity despite Ethereum's incumbency.
insights.quote: they have deterministic settlement which is actually an interesting characteristics that you know the L2s don't have um that from a regulatory perspective could create problems

insights.claim: Securitize holds roughly $400 million on its balance sheet plus liquid stock that it does not need for daily operations, and plans acquisitions of complementary capabilities and international licenses rather than direct tokenization competitors.
insights.speaker: Carlos Domingo
insights.so_what: Names Securitize as a funded acquirer in adjacent services and non-US licensed entities — private fund-services and licensed international platforms are the likely targets.
insights.quote: we have like $400 million or something like that on the balance sheet now plus liquid stock. we actually don't need that money to operate the business dayto day

insights.claim: Domingo sees convergence between RWAs and DeFi as a key expansion area because DeFi's existing digital-asset collateral has repeatedly caused problems through poor quality and hacks, making regulated real-world collateral the upgrade.
insights.speaker: Carlos Domingo
insights.so_what: Collateral quality is the pitch that gets RWAs into lending protocols — watch which DeFi venues onboard tokenized equities and treasuries as collateral first.
insights.quote: there is going to be a convergence of you know RWAS and DeFi. Today DeFi uses you know digital assets as collateral. As you know they've had a lot of problems precisely because of the the bad quality of collateral that gets hacked

insights.claim: Domingo does not view Robinhood as a competitor but as a distribution layer, and welcomes Robinhood Chain — built on Arbitrum technology Securitize supports — as a venue where Securitize could issue tokens for Robinhood to distribute.
insights.speaker: Carlos Domingo
insights.so_what: Maps the emerging stack split — Securitize as issuance infrastructure, Robinhood as retail distribution — rather than a head-to-head fight, which shapes how to value each.
insights.quote: I don't see Dood as a competitor. We talk to them all the time. I I think that they're more focused on distribution.

insights.claim: Domingo attributes memecoins outrunning RWAs on Robinhood Chain to RWAs' inherent adoption friction — they are often regulated instruments requiring KYC and understanding of what you own, whereas memecoin buyers are purely speculating.
insights.speaker: Carlos Domingo
insights.so_what: Sets realistic expectations: RWA adoption curves will lag speculative assets on any new chain, so early onchain volume mix is a poor predictor of long-term RWA traction.
insights.quote: I think RWAS you have more complexity in terms of adoption because in some cases are regulated as instruments. You might need KYC. You need to understand what you're buying.

insights.claim: Domingo expects tokenized IPOs to follow Robinhood's retail-IPO-access playbook — starting tiny with unknown companies, then scaling until every company does it — citing the large retail allocations in the SpaceX and Bullish offerings as the precedent.
insights.speaker: Carlos Domingo
insights.so_what: Gives an adoption template and timeline shape for tokenized primary issuance — expect a long, unglamorous ramp before it becomes a standard IPO tranche.
insights.quote: We're going to start with something. It's going to be small at the beginning um and then, you know, over time it's just going to become something that every single company does
